subtopic_detail: Croup severity assessment and dexamethasone dosing
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 2 year old boy is brought in by his mother at 2 am with a 1 day history of a barking cough and a hoarse voice.

On arrival he is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. He has a barking cough but no stridor when calm. Stridor becomes audible when he cries during examination. There is mild suprasternal recession only when upset, no tracheal tug at rest, and air entry is equal with no wheeze. He has taken a small amount of oral fluid in the last hour.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C. His immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 100/60 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; barking cough; hoarse voice; stridor only when crying; mild suprasternal recession when upset; air entry equal; no wheeze
data_table.History: 1 day symptoms; immunisations up to date; taking small oral fluids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, and discharge home once settled and tolerating fluids
options.rationale: This child has mild croup: stridor only when upset, no stridor at rest, no significant recession at rest. Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once is first line for mild and moderate croup and discharge is safe once the child is settled and taking fluids (Source: RCH CPG: Croup; TG Respiratory).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, and observe for 30 minutes before discharge
options.rationale: The dose is correct for mild croup, however observation for 30 minutes only applies when nebulised adrenaline has been given; for children receiving oral steroid alone the practice is to observe until settled and confirm oral tolerance (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days, and review with the general practitioner in the morning
options.rationale: Prednisolone is an alternative when dexamethasone is unavailable, however a single dexamethasone dose has a longer duration of action and is preferred; a 3 day course of prednisolone is not required and adds risk without benefit (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose, and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 immediately
options.rationale: The higher 0.6 mg/kg dose and nebulised adrenaline are reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession; using them for mild croup exposes the child to unnecessary tachycardia and mandates 3 hours of observation for rebound (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose, and admit for overnight observation of the airway
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is used only when the child cannot tolerate oral dexamethasone; it is second line to oral steroid, and admission for mild croup without stridor at rest is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: Mild croup is defined by a barking cough with no stridor at rest and no significant chest recession at rest, with the child alert. The Royal Children's guideline first line is a single oral dose of dexamethasone at 0.15 mg/kg with disposition home once the child is settled and tolerating oral fluids. The higher 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup, and nebulised adrenaline is added only for severe presentations. Any child who has received nebulised adrenaline requires a minimum of 3 hours of post administration observation before discharge to detect rebound obstruction.
key_points: Mild croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally once.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000.
Observe 3 hours after any nebulised adrenaline before discharge.
explanation.pearls: In Australian paediatric practice a single 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone dose provides 72 hours of anti-inflammatory effect and covers the natural history of most croup without needing repeat dosing.

stem:
You are the emergency department resident. An 18 month old boy weighing 12 kg presents with a 24 hour history of profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting. His older brother had similar symptoms last week.

On examination he is quiet but rousable and pushes the tongue depressor away appropriately. His mucous membranes are dry, his eyes are slightly sunken and his capillary refill is 2 seconds centrally. Skin turgor is mildly reduced and his peripheries are warm.

Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C. In triage he was given 4 mL/kg of oral rehydration solution by syringe every 5 minutes for 30 minutes but vomited the last two attempts. His urine output has been reduced but not absent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148/min; BP 92/58 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Rousable and interactive; dry mucous membranes; slightly sunken eyes; central capillary refill 2 sec; skin turgor mildly reduced; peripheries warm
data_table.History: 24 h watery diarrhoea and vomiting; sick contact; failed supervised oral trial in ED

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously as a bolus over 15 minutes, then reassess for further boluses guided by capillary refill
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is indicated for shock or severe dehydration with poor perfusion; this child has capillary refill 2 seconds, warm peripheries and no hypotension, so full bolus resuscitation is not required and risks unnecessary sodium load (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and give 20 mL/kg of oral rehydration solution over the first hour, then continue over 4 hours
options.rationale: The child has mild to moderate dehydration with failure of a supervised oral trial; the RCH pathway is nasogastric rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution as first line before moving to intravenous fluids, with equivalent efficacy and lower cost (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Give ondansetron 4 mg orally as a wafer and continue small volume oral rehydration by syringe, and reassess her hydration status in 60 minutes
options.rationale: Ondansetron 4 mg is the correct wafer dose for a 12 kg child and it does help vomiting, however after two vomits during a supervised oral trial the delivery route should be escalated rather than continued (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Insert an intravenous cannula and commence 5% dextrose with 0.45% sodium chloride at 46 mL per hour as maintenance
options.rationale: Intravenous fluids are second line to nasogastric rapid rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration; a maintenance only rate at 46 mL per hour also fails to address the fluid deficit and delays correction (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Admit for observation and offer oral rehydration solution ad libitum by the mother at the bedside and reassure her that most children improve with time
options.rationale: Ad libitum offering already failed at the point of care and admission without an active rehydration strategy is not appropriate; a structured nasogastric or intravenous regimen is required in the setting of ongoing vomiting (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

explanation.summary: For a child with mild to moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis who fails a supervised oral trial, nasogastric rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution is preferred before intravenous fluids. Nasogastric administration achieves comparable rehydration to intravenous fluids with fewer complications and shorter emergency stays. A single dose of ondansetron may reduce vomiting during the first hour. Intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock, ileus, or nasogastric failure.
key_points: Failed oral trial with mild to moderate dehydration: escalate to nasogastric before intravenous.
Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg once reduces vomiting in the first hour.
Reserve intravenous fluids for severe dehydration, shock, or nasogastric failure.
explanation.pearls: Nasogastric rapid rehydration delivers oral rehydration solution at 20 mL/kg in the first hour and completes replacement over 4 hours, matching intravenous outcomes at lower cost for children with ongoing vomiting.

subtopic_detail: Serious bacterial infection workup in neonates
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar overnight. A 25 day old girl born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery is brought in with a 6 hour history of poor feeding. Her mother noted her forehead felt hot 2 hours ago.

The baby is alert and moves her limbs symmetrically, tolerating handling. Her fontanelle is soft and flat, there is no rash and her peripheries are warm with capillary refill of 2 seconds. There has been no diarrhoea or cough, and her older brother has a runny nose.

Pulse rate 172/min, blood pressure 76/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98% on room air, rectal temperature 38.4 degrees C. Bloods drawn on arrival show white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (5.0-19.5), neutrophils 9.1 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 8 mg/L (less than 5), blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L, sodium and creatinine within normal limits. Urine dipstick from a clean catch shows leucocytes negative, nitrites negative. Nasopharyngeal aspirate is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 172/min; BP 76/40 mmHg; RR 44/min; SpO2 98% RA; rectal T 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; symmetric limb movement; fontanelle soft and flat; no rash; capillary refill 2 sec
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (5.0-19.5); neutrophils 9.1 x10^9/L; CRP 8 mg/L (<5); glucose 4.8 mmol/L; Na and creatinine within normal limits; urine dipstick leucs neg, nitrites neg; NPA pending
data_table.History: 25 days old; born 39 weeks NVD; 6 h poor feeding; sibling with URTI

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for observation, repeat blood cultures if fever persists, and start antibiotics only on further deterioration
options.rationale: Any infant under 4 weeks old with a fever above 38 degrees receives a full septic workup and empirical intravenous antibiotics without waiting for clinical deterioration because bacterial meningitis at this age presents with subtle signs (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Send a viral swab, wait for the nasopharyngeal aspirate result, and defer lumbar puncture if respiratory syncytial virus is positive
options.rationale: Identification of a viral cause does not exclude concurrent invasive bacterial infection in an infant under 4 weeks old; the septic workup and empirical antibiotics remain required (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture, take blood and urine cultures, and commence intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin empirically
options.rationale: Any infant under 4 weeks old with a fever above 38 degrees requires a full septic workup including lumbar puncture followed by empirical broad spectrum antibiotics; cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers the neonatal group of organisms including group B streptococcus, Listeria and Escherichia coli (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child; TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Give a single dose of ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg intramuscularly and discharge home with paediatric review in the morning
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin and is avoided in neonates under 1 month; more importantly no infant under 4 weeks with a fever is discharged without a full workup and inpatient antibiotic completion (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child; AMH Neonatal).

options.text: Perform a catheter urine specimen only, observe for 4 hours, and treat only when a bacterial cause is confirmed
options.rationale: A negative dipstick does not exclude urinary tract infection in young infants and observation only delays treatment; the required approach is lumbar puncture plus urine plus blood cultures followed by empirical antibiotics (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

explanation.summary: An infant under 4 weeks old with a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius receives a full septic workup including blood culture, urine by suprapubic aspirate or catheter, and lumbar puncture, then empirical intravenous antibiotics without waiting for deterioration. Cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers neonatal pathogens including group B streptococcus, Listeria monocytogenes and Escherichia coli. Ceftriaxone is avoided during the first month because it displaces bilirubin from albumin. A viral illness in an older sibling does not remove the need for the neonatal septic workup because concurrent bacterial infection remains possible.
key_points: Under 4 weeks and fever above 38 C: full septic workup plus empirical antibiotics.
Cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers group B streptococcus, Listeria and Escherichia coli.
Avoid ceftriaxone under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement risk.
explanation.pearls: In an infant under 28 days old use cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin rather than defaulting to ceftriaxone; the 28 day threshold is driven by the risk of kernicterus with ceftriaxone during the neonatal jaundice window.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation and admission decision
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3 month old ex 38 week boy who was brought in by his father with 4 days of coryza and 2 days of a wet cough. He had one apnoeic pause at home this morning during a feed.

In the department he is alert, in mild to moderate distress, with intercostal recession, tracheal tug, and diffuse fine crackles with expiratory wheeze. He has taken 60 percent of usual feeds today.

Pulse rate 168/min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 88% on room air rising to 92% on nasal prong at 2 L per minute after 20 minutes, temperature 37.4 degrees C. He remains tachypnoeic with recession at that flow. Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for respiratory syncytial virus. His weight is 5.2 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168/min; BP 88/52 mmHg; RR 62/min; SpO2 88% RA rising to 92% on 2 L/min nasal prong; T 37.4 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild to moderate distress; intercostal recession; tracheal tug; fine crackles bilaterally; expiratory wheeze
data_table.History: 3 months old; ex 38 weeks; 4 days coryza; one apnoea at home; 60% feeds; NPA RSV positive; weight 5.2 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Continue low flow nasal prong oxygen at 2 L per minute and reassess response after a further 2 hours
options.rationale: Low flow nasal prong is the correct first line oxygen delivery, however this infant is still tachypnoeic with recession and has already had an apnoea at home; a further 2 hour delay before escalation is inappropriate given the risk profile (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 5 mg back to back and reassess in 30 minutes before deciding on admission
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended in infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis; there is no evidence of benefit and it may cause tachycardia and tachyphylaxis (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Administer nebulised hypertonic 3 percent sodium chloride and reassess work of breathing after 30 minutes
options.rationale: Nebulised hypertonic sodium chloride has been removed from the RCH pathway; systematic reviews do not show meaningful benefit in bronchiolitis (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg per minute with a target SpO2 of 90 percent and admit to the paediatric ward
options.rationale: High flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg per minute is appropriate for a bronchiolitic infant who has failed low flow oxygen with ongoing work of breathing, with an SpO2 target of 90 percent to avoid oxygen toxicity; admission to a monitored bed is required given the reported apnoea (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PREDICT bronchiolitis guideline 2022).

options.text: Intubate and ventilate now with a size 3.5 uncuffed endotracheal tube given the reported apnoea at home
options.rationale: Intubation is not first line here; the infant is oxygenating adequately on low flow oxygen and non invasive support with high flow has not been trialled, so early intubation is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: In bronchiolitis with hypoxia the Royal Children's approach is to start with low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L per minute and escalate to high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg per minute if low flow fails after around 2 hours or the child has red flag features. The SpO2 target on the guideline is 90 percent to avoid hyperoxia and unnecessary escalation. Salbutamol, hypertonic sodium chloride and nebulised adrenaline are not routinely recommended in infants under 12 months old. A history of apnoea, prematurity or feeding failure lowers the threshold for admission and closer monitoring.
key_points: Low flow oxygen first, high flow at 2 L/kg per minute if failing.
SpO2 target 90 percent for bronchiolitis at RCH.
Salbutamol, hypertonic saline and nebulised adrenaline not recommended in under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: A reported apnoea in a young infant with bronchiolitis mandates a monitored bed and lowered SpO2 target of 90 percent, even when the child appears clinically stable at triage.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and reporting of suspected non-accidental injury
stem:
You are the paediatric resident in a rural emergency department. A 5 month old boy is brought in by his mother's partner for reduced arm movement noted since a nappy change 2 hours ago. There is no reported witnessed fall.

On examination he is alert but grimacing when the right upper limb is moved. There is bruising over the right upper arm, three small circular bruises over the left cheek, and a healing linear mark on the left thigh. His head circumference is on the 50th centile; his weight has fallen from the 25th to the 3rd centile since the 4 month check.

Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C. Right humerus radiograph shows a mid shaft spiral fracture. His developmental milestones per parental report include rolling at 4 months. He has one older half sibling in out of home care.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148/min; BP 84/50 mmHg; RR 34/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; grimaces on right upper limb movement; bruising right upper arm; three circular bruises left cheek; healing linear mark left thigh; head circumference 50th centile; weight falls from 25th to 3rd centile
data_table.Investigations: Right humerus radiograph: mid shaft spiral fracture
data_table.History: 5 months old; no witnessed fall; sibling in out of home care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Refer to the community child health nurse for a home visit and weight review within the week for reassessment before any further imaging or bloods are arranged
options.rationale: This is a red flag presentation for physical abuse with a spiral fracture in a non ambulant child, unexplained bruising in different sites, and faltering growth; a community follow up alone would leave the child at ongoing risk (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.text: Discharge the child with the mother's partner after immobilising the arm and give general practitioner review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Discharge before a child protection workup risks further harm; a suspected non accidental injury requires admission and formal safeguarding assessment before disposition (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.text: Order a skeletal survey and coagulation screen only, and discharge home when normal to await outpatient results with paediatric review of the results the next day
options.rationale: Ordering the tests without safeguarding action is inadequate; mandatory notification to child protection services and involvement of paediatric team are required whenever non accidental injury is suspected in a child under 2 years (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.text: Consult orthopaedics for a definitive plan of the humeral fracture and defer safeguarding until fracture management is clarified
options.rationale: Fracture management does not take priority over safeguarding; the safeguarding pathway runs in parallel and is a mandatory reporting obligation for the doctor at the point of suspicion (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.text: Admit the infant for a full child protection workup, notify child protection services now, and consult the paediatric team
options.rationale: A spiral humeral fracture in a non ambulant infant with additional unexplained bruises and faltering growth is highly suggestive of physical abuse; an admission for a skeletal survey, retinal examination, coagulation screen and social assessment, mandatory notification to child protection services, and paediatric team involvement is the correct standard of care (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury; RCH CPG: Child abuse).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

explanation.summary: A spiral long bone fracture in a non ambulant infant, together with bruises on multiple non bony sites and faltering growth, is a classic non accidental injury pattern that requires admission for a full child protection workup and mandatory notification to child protection services. The workup includes skeletal survey, retinal examination for haemorrhages, coagulation screen and social assessment. Mandatory notification obligations for doctors apply once there is a reasonable suspicion of harm, not once harm is proven. Delaying disposition until the fracture is orthopaedically fixed is not appropriate because safeguarding runs in parallel with medical care.
key_points: Spiral fracture in a non ambulant child: mandatory child protection referral.
Full workup: skeletal survey, retinal examination, coagulation screen, social assessment.
Reasonable suspicion, not proof, triggers the mandatory notification duty.
explanation.pearls: Bruising in a pre cruising infant (less than about 9 months old) is uncommon from normal activity, so any bruise in a non ambulant infant warrants a low threshold for a safeguarding assessment before discharge.

sources.label: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

subtopic_detail: Prolonged neonatal jaundice with pale stools
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general paediatric clinic. A 4 week old girl is brought in by her mother because of ongoing yellow skin since discharge from hospital. She was breastfed exclusively, born at 39 weeks weighing 3.2 kg. She had physiological jaundice on day 3 which did not require phototherapy.

On examination she is alert, feeding well and back to her birth weight. Sclerae and skin appear icteric to the mid abdomen. The abdomen is soft with no palpable liver edge. Her mother reports her stools have become pale over the last 10 days and her urine has been dark yellow.

Pulse rate 138/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Blood total bilirubin 148 micromol/L (less than 20), direct bilirubin 62 micromol/L, ALT 78 U/L (less than 45), GGT 320 U/L (less than 60), full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138/min; BP 78/44 mmHg; RR 42/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; icteric to mid abdomen; abdomen soft; no palpable liver edge; feeding well; back to birth weight
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L (<20); direct bilirubin 62 micromol/L; ALT 78 U/L (<45); GGT 320 U/L (<60); FBC within normal limits; thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.History: 4 weeks old; exclusively breastfed; pale stools 10 days; dark urine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents that the presentation is consistent with breast milk jaundice and review clinically in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and resolves without pale stools; a direct bilirubin fraction above 17 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total in a 4 week old requires urgent workup for cholestasis and cannot be reassured (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN cholestasis guideline).

options.text: Arrange urgent same day paediatric admission for further workup and a hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan and hepatology review
options.rationale: A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a 4 week old with pale stools and dark urine is a surgical emergency until biliary atresia is excluded; the Kasai portoenterostomy outcome is much better if performed before 60 days of age, so same day paediatric admission for urgent workup and hepatology review is required (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN cholestasis guideline).

options.text: Commence phototherapy in the clinic and arrange repeat total bilirubin in 24 hours to guide further care
options.rationale: Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; it is ineffective and inappropriate for conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and delays definitive workup (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular vitamin K 1 mg and repeat coagulation studies before referral
options.rationale: While correcting vitamin K status is part of cholestatic workup, a single injection alone without paediatric referral misses the time critical requirement to exclude biliary atresia within the first 60 days (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Advise a trial of formula feeding for 48 hours and repeat total bilirubin to distinguish breast milk jaundice
options.rationale: A formula trial is used only in stable unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; it has no place when the direct fraction is elevated and there are pale stools, and it delays the diagnosis of biliary atresia (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

explanation.summary: A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in an infant beyond 2 weeks old with pale stools and dark urine must be treated as a surgical emergency until biliary atresia is excluded. Urgent same day admission for hepatology review, imaging including hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan and possibly cholangiography allows the Kasai portoenterostomy to be performed before 60 days of age when outcomes are markedly better. Phototherapy is only useful for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does not treat the biliary obstruction. A formula trial is appropriate only for stable unconjugated jaundice and should not delay workup in a cholestatic infant.
key_points: Direct bilirubin above 17 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total is always abnormal.
Pale stools plus dark urine in an infant is biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days gives the best outcomes.
explanation.pearls: In any infant beyond 2 weeks of age with persistent jaundice, always split the bilirubin; a conjugated fraction over 17 micromol/L makes biliary atresia the working diagnosis until same day imaging and hepatology review say otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes with 75 g OGTT
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 32 year old primigravida at 27 weeks of pregnancy. Her booking body mass index was 31 kg/m squared and her mother has type 2 diabetes. She had a raised random glucose of 8.4 mmol/L at booking.

Her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks returns with fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L (less than 5.1), 1 hour glucose 9.8 mmol/L (less than 10.0), 2 hour glucose 8.6 mmol/L (less than 8.5). She has been feeling well with no polyuria or polydipsia. She reports foetal movements are appropriate.

Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Foetal heart rate 148/min. Symphysis fundal height 27 cm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82/min; BP 118/76 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C; FHR 148/min
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 27 cm; foetal movements appropriate
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1); 1 hour 9.8 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 8.6 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.History: Primigravida at 27 weeks; BMI 31; mother has T2DM; booking random glucose 8.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: The result is within normal limits and no further glucose testing is required for the remainder of pregnancy
options.rationale: Two of the three OGTT values are above the threshold; even a single value above the cut off establishes gestational diabetes under the Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society criteria (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022; RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy).

options.text: The result is suggestive of type 2 diabetes preceding pregnancy and a HbA1c should be requested to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy is defined by a fasting value at or above 7 mmol/L or a 2 hour value at or above 11.1 mmol/L; these values fall in the gestational diabetes range, not the overt diabetes range (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022).

options.text: The result meets criteria for gestational diabetes and she should be referred to a multidisciplinary diabetes in pregnancy service
options.rationale: The fasting value of 5.4 mmol/L and the 2 hour value of 8.6 mmol/L both exceed the ADIPS thresholds; any single elevated value establishes gestational diabetes and requires referral to a multidisciplinary team for dietary review, home glucose monitoring and consideration of pharmacotherapy (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022; RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy).

options.text: The result is borderline and the OGTT should be repeated in 4 weeks before starting any interventions
options.rationale: The ADIPS criteria do not require repeat testing when a value exceeds threshold; delaying management by 4 weeks worsens obstetric outcomes and is not standard care (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022).

options.text: The result is normal but she should commence metformin because of the family history of type 2 diabetes
options.rationale: Metformin is not prescribed prophylactically in pregnancy based on family history alone; treatment is guided by glycaemic targets after diagnosis (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022).

explanation.summary: Under the Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society criteria, gestational diabetes is diagnosed on a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test when the fasting value is at or above 5.1 mmol/L, the 1 hour value is at or above 10.0 mmol/L, or the 2 hour value is at or above 8.5 mmol/L. Any single elevated value is sufficient for diagnosis. Overt diabetes in pregnancy requires a fasting value at or above 7.0 mmol/L or a 2 hour value at or above 11.1 mmol/L. Once gestational diabetes is diagnosed, referral to a multidisciplinary diabetes in pregnancy team is standard for dietary review, home monitoring and pharmacotherapy decisions.
key_points: ADIPS cut offs: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L.
Any single value at or above threshold diagnoses gestational diabetes.
Referral to a multidisciplinary diabetes in pregnancy service is standard.
explanation.pearls: In Australia the ADIPS 75 g OGTT cut offs are lower than the WHO 1999 values, so fasting 5.1 mmol/L is the diagnostic threshold rather than 5.5 mmol/L; even a single elevated point mandates management referral.

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic sequencing in primary postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a birth suite. A 34 year old primigravida has had a normal vaginal delivery at 40 weeks of a live infant. She has an estimated blood loss of 900 mL 12 minutes after birth with an atonic uterus felt above the umbilicus. Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly was given at delivery of the anterior shoulder.

She is anxious but alert. Bimanual uterine massage has been started, an intravenous cannula placed, cross match is sent and 1 g of tranexamic acid intravenously has been given. Her bladder is empty via urinary catheter. Placenta appears complete on inspection.

Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C. She has no known allergies and no history of asthma or hypertension.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; atonic uterus above umbilicus; bimanual massage started; placenta complete on inspection; bladder empty
data_table.Interventions: Oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery; IV access; cross match sent; tranexamic acid 1 g IV given
data_table.History: Primigravida; 40 week NVD; no asthma or hypertension; no allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to administer?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intravenously as a slow push and repeat the dose after 5 minutes if uterine tone remains poor
options.rationale: Ergometrine is a reasonable second line uterotonic where blood pressure is controlled, however guidelines recommend a further oxytocin bolus or infusion before ergometrine because oxytocin remains the first line drug (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

options.text: Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle and repeat every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses if bleeding continues
options.rationale: Carboprost is used when oxytocin and ergometrine have failed to achieve tone; it is contraindicated in known asthma and is a later step in the sequence rather than the immediate next drug (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

options.text: Misoprostol 800 micrograms per rectum as a single dose and reassess uterine tone after 30 minutes with continued bimanual massage
options.rationale: Misoprostol per rectum has a slower onset than intravenous oxytocin; it is used when intravenous access is delayed or as an adjunct after other uterotonics rather than as the immediate first line intravenous drug (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

options.text: Oxytocin 5 units intravenously as a slow push, followed by an oxytocin infusion of 40 units in 1 litre of Hartmann's over 4 hours
options.rationale: After an atonic postpartum haemorrhage exceeding 500 mL despite prophylactic intramuscular oxytocin, the RANZCOG algorithm is a further slow intravenous oxytocin bolus followed by a maintenance infusion; ergometrine and carboprost are added if uterine tone does not respond (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

options.text: Repeat oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh and continue bimanual uterine massage while awaiting further intravenous access
options.rationale: Intramuscular oxytocin has slower onset than intravenous; when intravenous access is present the intravenous route with an infusion is preferred and repeat intramuscular dosing is a step backwards (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

explanation.summary: In primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony the RANZCOG algorithm is bimanual uterine massage plus tranexamic acid plus a stepwise sequence of uterotonics beginning with further oxytocin. A slow intravenous bolus of 5 units of oxytocin is followed by an intravenous oxytocin infusion at 40 units per litre over 4 hours. Ergometrine 250 micrograms is added second line when hypertension is not a concern. Carboprost is the third line uterotonic and is contraindicated in asthma; misoprostol is an option if intravenous access is delayed.
key_points: Oxytocin bolus plus infusion is the first drug after prophylactic dose has failed.
Ergometrine second line; avoid in hypertension.
Carboprost third line; contraindicated in asthma.
explanation.pearls: After a prophylactic 10 unit intramuscular oxytocin dose fails, give a further 5 unit slow intravenous bolus and immediately begin a 40 unit per litre infusion at 250 mL per hour before moving to ergometrine.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28 year old primigravida at 33 weeks. She was referred from clinic 3 hours ago with headache and epigastric pain. She has known pre-eclampsia diagnosed 4 days earlier and is on labetalol 200 mg orally twice daily.

On examination she is alert with mild epigastric tenderness. Reflexes are brisk with no clonus. Foetal heart rate is normal on cardiotocography.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 172/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat manual measurement, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Bloods show haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), ALT 68 U/L (less than 35), urinary protein creatinine ratio 45 mg/mmol (less than 30). Foetal heart rate 142/min. She has been given 4 g magnesium sulfate intravenous loading dose.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 172/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat; RR 18/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 36.7 C; FHR 142/min
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild epigastric tenderness; brisk reflexes; no clonus; CTG normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L (115-165); platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.35); ALT 68 U/L (<35); UPCR 45 mg/mmol (<30)
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg orally BD; magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate blood pressure management?

options.text: Increase her oral labetalol to 400 mg three times daily and recheck the blood pressure in 60 minutes
options.rationale: An oral dose adjustment is too slow for a systolic blood pressure at or above 170 or diastolic at or above 110 mmHg; parenteral antihypertensive treatment is required within 30 to 60 minutes to reduce the risk of maternal stroke (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023; RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy).

options.text: Aim to reduce the blood pressure to less than 130/80 mmHg within the first hour using an intravenous nitroprusside infusion
options.rationale: An aggressive target below 130/80 mmHg risks compromising uteroplacental perfusion, and nitroprusside is not used in pregnancy due to foetal cyanide toxicity (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023).

options.text: Give intravenous methyldopa 250 mg and repeat magnesium sulfate 4 g loading intravenous dose
options.rationale: Methyldopa is not available intravenously in Australian formularies and is a slow onset oral agent; repeat magnesium loading is not indicated because the maintenance infusion should follow the loading dose (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023).

options.text: Perform emergency caesarean section as the definitive treatment before controlling the blood pressure
options.rationale: Blood pressure must be controlled before delivery to avoid a maternal stroke during anaesthesia and the peripartum period; delivery is the definitive treatment but is undertaken after acute stabilisation (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023).

options.text: Give intravenous labetalol 20 mg as a slow push and repeat every 10 minutes titrated to blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg
options.rationale: In severe hypertension of pregnancy at or above 170/110 mmHg the SOMANZ algorithm targets a blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg within 30 to 60 minutes using intravenous labetalol 20 mg with 10 minute repeats up to 300 mg total, or intravenous hydralazine or oral nifedipine (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023; RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension of pregnancy at or above 170 systolic or 110 diastolic mmHg is a hypertensive emergency requiring parenteral treatment within 30 to 60 minutes to reduce stroke risk. The SOMANZ options are intravenous labetalol 20 mg with 10 minute repeats up to 300 mg, intravenous hydralazine, or oral immediate release nifedipine. The target is a blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg while preserving uteroplacental perfusion, not normotension. Magnesium sulfate is given concurrently for eclampsia prophylaxis and delivery is planned once the mother is stabilised.
key_points: Severe range starts at 170/110 mmHg and needs parenteral treatment.
Target below 160/110 mmHg in 30 to 60 minutes.
Nitroprusside is contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: In pregnancy avoid ACE inhibitors, ARBs, atenolol and nitroprusside; the safe parenteral agents are labetalol and hydralazine, and immediate release oral nifedipine is a useful ward option when intravenous access is limited.

stem:
You are the obstetric resident reviewing a 26 year old primigravida at 9 weeks of pregnancy in the emergency department. She has had 3 weeks of daily vomiting with weight loss of 4.5 kg from a pre pregnancy weight of 68 kg. She has tried pyridoxine and doxylamine at home without benefit.

She looks unwell with a dry mouth and mild epigastric tenderness. Ketones are 3 on urinalysis, ultrasound at 8 weeks confirmed an intrauterine singleton pregnancy with foetal heart activity.

Pulse rate 108/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C. Bloods show sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 8.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), TSH 0.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 within normal limits. She has been able to take small sips of water only in the last 24 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108/min; BP 104/62 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Dry mouth; mild epigastric tenderness; urinary ketones 3
data_table.Investigations: Na 132 mmol/L (135-145); K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); urea 8.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5); creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90); TSH 0.4 mIU/L; free T4 within normal limits; ultrasound: singleton intrauterine pregnancy with FHR
data_table.History: Primigravida 9 weeks; 4.5 kg weight loss; failed pyridoxine and doxylamine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous rehydration with 0.9% sodium chloride plus potassium replacement, thiamine 100 mg intravenously and ondansetron 4 mg intravenously
options.rationale: The RANZCOG hyperemesis pathway admits for intravenous fluids using 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's with potassium replacement, thiamine 100 mg intravenously to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and an antiemetic such as ondansetron 4 mg intravenously as first line escalation (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019; TG Obstetric).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

options.text: Discharge with an oral course of prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days and general practitioner review the next day with instructions to return if vomiting recurs or fluid intake fails
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after inpatient intravenous therapy has failed; oral prednisolone as a first line in a dehydrated hypokalaemic patient is not standard care (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular metoclopramide 10 mg and reassess before deciding on admission or discharge with an oral rehydration trial before deciding on disposition
options.rationale: A single antiemetic dose does not address the intravascular volume loss, ketonuria and hypokalaemia; intravenous rehydration with electrolyte correction is required (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

options.text: Commence 5 percent dextrose infusion at maintenance rate and add pyridoxine 25 mg orally three times daily with regular antiemetic review over the next 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Dextrose without prior thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in a malnourished pregnant patient; 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's are preferred as the initial fluid with thiamine given first (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

options.text: Arrange dilation and evacuation of the pregnancy given the severity of her symptoms and weight loss and refer to social work for support and information about future options
options.rationale: Termination is not standard care for hyperemesis; effective escalation of antiemetic therapy achieves symptom control in the majority of patients (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum with intractable vomiting, weight loss over 5 percent of pre pregnancy weight, ketonuria and electrolyte disturbance requires admission for intravenous rehydration. First line fluids are 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's with potassium replacement guided by serum potassium, and thiamine 100 mg intravenously must be given before any dextrose to avoid Wernicke encephalopathy. First line antiemetics are pyridoxine and doxylamine; ondansetron and metoclopramide are used when the first line agents have failed. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory cases after inpatient escalation has failed.
key_points: 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's plus potassium as first line fluid.
Thiamine 100 mg intravenously precedes any dextrose in malnourished patients.
Corticosteroids only after conventional antiemetic escalation fails.
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine 100 mg intravenously daily for at least 3 days before dextrose in any pregnant patient with sustained vomiting and weight loss, otherwise a glucose load risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.

sources.label: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019
